Design an alternative to the night light, alarm, relay trainer, or traffic light. Choice does not remove the engineering requirements: the project still needs a safe circuit, Linux/Python evidence, measurements, staged tests, and a documented revision.

::: {.callout-warning title="Approval comes before purchasing or wiring"}
Do not buy parts, connect a board, reserve a high-current load, or begin a powered build until the teacher approves the problem, schematic, bill of materials, interface voltages, budget, fallback, and test plan.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Safety boundary"}
Student wiring remains at protected extra-low voltage. An approved driver and separate protected supply are required for any load beyond a low-current indicator. Never connect a signal to GPIO or an analogue input until its worst-case voltage has been documented and measured within the exact board limit.
:::

## Choose a level

| Level | Scope | Minimum evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Minimum | One protected input, one low-current output, and a small Linux/Python behaviour | Schematic, I/O table, measurements, three tests |
| Proficient | A state machine or adjustable decision, event evidence, and one driver/interface stage | State table, calculations, log or graph, fault diagnosis |
| Extension | A second sensor/output, data analysis, relay-controlled load, or carefully justified new component | Datasheet-based interface design and additional validation |

The teacher may reduce an unsafe or oversized proposal to a smaller approved version.

## Non-negotiable constraints

1. All student wiring uses protected extra-low voltage.
2. The exact controller, sensor, and output limits are documented before connection.
3. GPIO does not directly power motors, relay coils, lamps, solenoids, or horns.
4. Analogue input voltage remains within the exact board limit under normal conditions and one credible fault.
5. A teacher-approved schematic and BOM exist before power-up.
6. The minimum version uses parts already available or a confirmed fallback.
7. The project can be tested in small independent stages.
8. Linux/Python is functional, not decorative.
9. Success criteria are measurable within the available class time.
10. Public portfolio evidence contains no credentials, private network data, faces without approval, or real security details.

## Suitable project directions

| Input idea | Output/behaviour idea | Interface question to resolve |
|---|---|---|
| Pushbutton, limit switch, magnetic contact | LED pattern, timer, counter, alarm model | Pull-up/pull-down and debounce |
| Approved digital light, temperature, or distance sensor | Threshold indicator or event log | Supply, logic level, bus, and library |
| Potentiometer or analogue sensor | Bar graph or threshold control | ADC maximum and divider design |
| Two switches | Reaction game or access/interlock model | Stable idle state and state machine |
| Approved moisture or environmental module | Reminder or warning model | Corrosion, output range, calibration |
| Keyboard or simulated input | Full software prototype while hardware is unavailable | Clear later hardware adapter |

Examples are starting points, not pre-approved circuits. Modules with the same product name may contain different regulators and pull-ups.

## Problem and success criteria

Write one sentence:

> We will design a __________________ that uses __________________ to __________________.

Then write four to six numbered criteria. Include:

- one input-response time or threshold;
- one electrical limit;
- one repeatability requirement;
- one safe power-up/shutdown requirement;
- one documentation or logging requirement.

## Approval gates

### Gate 1: proposal

- problem and users are clear;
- success criteria are measurable;
- minimum version fits the time and budget;
- fallback is named.

### Gate 2: documentation

- exact datasheets or official platform documentation are linked;
- supply, GPIO, ADC, and load limits are recorded;
- pinouts are verified from the exact parts.

### Gate 3: schematic and calculations

- source, protection, input, controller, driver, output, and return are visible;
- resistor, divider, current, power, or timing calculations are complete;
- test points and safe state are labelled.

### Gate 4: staged test

- software logic runs with simulated input;
- sensor is tested without the controller when appropriate;
- output/driver is tested separately;
- measured interface voltage is safe before connection.

### Gate 5: integration

- teacher performs a power-off inspection;
- initial power uses current limiting;
- minimum function is demonstrated before extensions begin.

| Test ID | Requirement | Setup and input | Expected result | Measurement/log needed | Stop condition |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Safe power-up |  |  |  | Heat, smell, supply limiting, unexpected voltage |
| T2 | Normal case |  |  |  |  |
| T3 | Boundary case |  |  |  |  |
| T4 | Repeatability | Repeat three times |  |  |  |
| T5 | Prepared fault | Teacher-approved open/disconnected input |  |  |  |
| T6 | Safe shutdown | Stop program and remove load power | Outputs off | Voltage or observation |  |

## Troubleshooting guide

1. Stop and remove load power before moving wiring.
2. Reduce the system to the last stage that worked.
3. State one hypothesis; do not replace several parts at once.
4. Choose one measurement or software observation that separates two possible causes.
5. Record expected and observed evidence.
6. Change one variable and repeat the same test.
7. Restore the safe state before reconnecting the next stage.

| Symptom | Evidence to collect first |
|---|---|
| No sensor data | Sensor supply, device detection, pinout, and raw read error |
| Random input | Input-node voltage, pull resistor, contact stability |
| Code works in simulation but not hardware | Raw GPIO/sensor state before project logic |
| Controller resets when load activates | Supply voltage before/during activation; driver and return paths |
| Output always active | Driver polarity and safe-state command |
| Values make no physical sense | Units, range, calibration, raw value, and datasheet definition |

## Fallback if parts fail to arrive

Every proposal selects one:

1. replace the missing sensor with a pushbutton or potentiometer using an approved interface;
2. run the same state machine with keyboard or synthetic input and document the hardware adapter;
3. build the automatic night light, Linux alarm, or traffic-light core using class stock;
4. complete a measured subsystem and a simulated integration, clearly labelled as such.

The fallback must still produce circuit, Linux/Python, testing, and portfolio evidence.

## Exact portfolio evidence

1. approved proposal, selected level, and success criteria;
2. approved BOM with actual costs or confirmed stock status;
3. official documentation for every electrical interface;
4. original system block diagram and circuit schematic;
5. calculations and stated assumptions;
6. completed interface table and pre-connection voltage evidence;
7. software state diagram, flowchart, or clear behavioural description;
8. completed test table with at least three trials;
9. one fault, hypothesis, diagnostic measurement, change, and retest;
10. relevant code or log excerpt;
11. conclusion against each criterion, limitations, and next step;
12. source attribution and a privacy check.

Do not represent simulated, example, or predicted values as physical measurements.

## Authoritative sources

Use the manufacturer datasheet for the exact sensor and driver, the official documentation for the exact controller, and the Python standard-library documentation for software features. For a BeagleBone Black, begin with the [official board overview](https://docs.beagleboard.org/boards/beaglebone/black/ch04.html) and [connector reference](https://docs.beagleboard.org/boards/beaglebone/black/ch07.html).
